title: Macropinocytosis-mediated recyclable LYTACs (McR-TACs) for receptor-independent protein degradation - Nature Biotechnology
gist: University of Wisconsin-Madison researchers developed McR-TACs, a new class of lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) that use a polyzwitterion instead of a receptor-binding ligand to trigger macropinocytosis, making the degrader receptor-independent and recyclable via a dissociate-and-exocytose mechanism, and showed it durably degrades PD-L1 and MIF and shrinks tumors in a triple-negative breast cancer mouse model — with a patent already filed.

themes.theme: A new recyclable, receptor-independent mechanism for targeted protein degradation

insights.claim: Conventional LYTACs (lysosome-targeting chimeras) are limited by being nonrecyclable and receptor-dependent, meaning each degrader molecule is consumed after one round of shuttling its target protein to the lysosome and requires a specific cell-surface receptor to enter the cell, restricting the modality's broader use.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: This is the core unmet need in the extracellular/membrane targeted protein degradation field that the paper's innovation addresses — investors tracking the TPD space should note receptor-dependence and non-recyclability as the standing bottleneck competitors are trying to solve.
insights.quote: The degradation of cell membrane and extracellular proteins with lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) is limited by nonrecyclable, receptor-dependent mechanisms

insights.claim: The researchers engineered McR-TACs (macropinocytosis-mediated recyclable LYTACs), chimeras built from a polyzwitterion conjugated to a protein-of-interest (POI) ligand, which trigger macropinocytosis (a receptor-independent, bulk fluid-uptake pathway) to enter cells together with the target protein, rather than relying on a specific surface receptor.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Receptor-independence broadens the addressable target universe for this degrader modality to proteins/cell types that lack a convenient endocytic receptor, a design principle competing TPD companies would need to match or differentiate against.
insights.locator: Here we developed a recyclable chimera composed of a polyzwitterion and protein of interest (POI) ligand

insights.claim: The McR-TAC chimera dissociates from its target protein in the acidic endocytic compartment, then is exocytosed back to the cell surface via the endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transcytosis pathway, allowing the same degrader molecule to initiate additional rounds of target protein degradation rather than being destroyed after a single use.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A catalytic, recyclable degrader could achieve durable target suppression at lower and less frequent dosing than single-use degraders, a potential pharmacokinetic and cost-of-goods advantage relevant to dosing strategy and differentiation versus first-generation LYTACs.
insights.quote: it can dissociate from the POI in the acidic endocytic compartments and subsequently be exocytosed through the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi transcytosis pathway

insights.claim: McR-TAC-induced macropinocytosis and degradation efficiency positively correlate with cellular RAS expression levels across multiple cell lines (4T1-hPD-L1, U87, BxPC-3, MDA-MB-231, PANC-1, Caco-2), with an R2 of 0.83 between RAS expression and dextran uptake, and MIF degradation was reduced upon KRAS knockdown.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A RAS-expression-dependent mechanism suggests McR-TACs could be preferentially potent in RAS/KRAS-driven cancers (a large and commercially important tumor category including pancreatic and lung cancers), which is a specific translational hypothesis worth tracking in follow-on studies.
insights.locator: Extended Data Fig. 6 The protein degradation effects of McR-TACs in different cell lines positively correlates with RAS expression levels

themes.theme: Efficacy against membrane and extracellular targets in a cancer model

insights.claim: McR-TACs durably degraded both a cell membrane protein target (PD-L1, an immune checkpoint) and a secreted extracellular protein target (macrophage migration inhibitory factor, MIF) in a triple-negative breast cancer mouse model, and this degradation inhibited tumor growth.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Demonstrating in vivo efficacy against a validated immuno-oncology target (PD-L1) is a direct signal of translational relevance to cancer immunotherapy, positioning McR-TACs as a potential complement or alternative to antibody-based checkpoint blockade.
insights.quote: These macropinocytosis-mediated recyclable LYTACs (McR-TACs) durably degrade the cell membrane protein (programmed cell death ligand 1) or the extracellular protein (macrophage migration inhibitory factor) in a triple-negative breast cancer mouse model, thereby inhibiting the tumor growth.

insights.claim: The paper reports that McR-TAC-mediated protein degradation enhances antitumor immune responses in vivo through targeted protein degradation, as summarized in the figure describing solid tumor growth suppression.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Coupling protein degradation with an active immune-response boost (rather than passive target removal alone) suggests a potential combination mechanism-of-action advantage over degradation-only or blockade-only competitor approaches.
insights.quote: McR-TACs suppress solid tumor growth and enhance antitumor immune responses through TPD in vivo

insights.claim: The corresponding author (Quanyin Hu) and first author (Peixin Liu) have submitted a patent application related to the McR-TAC findings described in this manuscript.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: An active patent filing signals the authors and University of Wisconsin-Madison see near-term commercial/IP value in the McR-TAC platform, a concrete marker for tracking potential licensing deals or spinout activity in the targeted protein degradation space.
insights.quote: Q.H. and P.L. have submitted a patent application related to the findings in this manuscript.

themes.theme: Positioning within the broader targeted protein degradation landscape

insights.claim: The paper situates McR-TACs within a growing family of extracellular/membrane protein degrader approaches referenced in its citations, including the original LYTAC concept (Banik et al., Nature 2020), CYpHER catalytic degraders, FcRn-mediated cycling LYTACs, and CD44-assisted transcytosable chimeras, framing extracellular targeted protein degradation as an actively expanding drug discovery modality.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The competitive field for recyclable/catalytic extracellular degraders is already crowded with multiple named approaches (CYpHER, FcRn-cycling LYTACs, transcytosable chimeras), indicating investors should view McR-TACs as one of several competing platform bets rather than a category of one.
